{{nihongo|'''Akira Yoshizawa'''|吉澤 章|Yoshizawa Akira|14 March 1911&nbsp;– 14 March 2005}} was a Japanese origamist, considered to be the grandmaster of [[origami]]. He is credited with raising origami from a craft to a living art. According to his own estimation made in 1989, he created more than 50,000 models, of which only a few hundred designs were presented as diagrams in his 18 books. Yoshizawa acted as an international cultural ambassador for Japan throughout his career. In 1983, [[Emperor of Japan|Emperor]] [[Hirohito]] awarded him the [[Order of the Rising Sun]], 5th class, one of the highest honors bestowed in Japan.<ref name="times-obit">{{cite web |url=http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/comment/obituaries/article439880.ece |title=Akira Yoshizawa – Origami artist of stunning originality who became an ambassador for Japanese culture and his art |work=[[The Times]] |date=30 March 2005 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110522231312/http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/comment/obituaries/article439880.ece |archive-date=22 May 2011 |access-date=4 April 2021}}</ref>

== Life ==
Yoshizawa was born on 14 March 1911, in [[Kaminokawa, Tochigi|Kaminokawa]], Japan, to the family of a dairy farmer. When he was a child, he took pleasure in teaching himself origami. He moved into a factory job in [[Tokyo]] when he was 13 years old. His passion for origami was rekindled in his early 20s, when he was promoted from factory worker to technical draftsman. His new job was to teach junior employees geometry. Yoshizawa used the traditional art of origami to understand and communicate geometrical problems.<ref name="times-obit" />

In 1937, he left factory work to pursue origami full-time. During the next 20 years, he lived in total poverty, earning his living by door-to-door selling of {{Transliteration|ja|[[tsukudani]]}} (a Japanese preserved condiment that is usually made of seaweed). During World War II, Yoshizawa served in the army medical corps in Hong Kong. He made origami models to cheer up the sick patients, but eventually fell ill himself and was sent back to Japan.<ref name = "About">{{Citation | publisher = About | title = Origami | contribution = Akira Yoshizawa | type = biography | url = http://origami.about.com/od/History-Of-Origami/a/Akira-Yoshizawa-Origami-Biography.htm | access-date = 2012-03-14 | archive-date = 2016-08-03 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160803213301/http://origami.about.com/od/History-Of-Origami/a/Akira-Yoshizawa-Origami-Biography.htm | url-status = dead }}.</ref>  His origami work was creative enough to be included in the 1944 book ''Origami Shuko'', by {{nihongo|[[Isao Honda]]|本多 功}}. However, it was his work for the January 1952 issue of the magazine ''[[Asahi Graph]]'' that launched his career, which included the 12 zodiac signs commissioned by a magazine.<ref name="times-obit" />

In 1954, his first monograph, ''Atarashii Origami Geijutsu'' (New Origami Art) was published. In this work, he established the [[Yoshizawa–Randlett system]] of notation for origami folds (a system of symbols, arrows and diagrams<ref name = "PBS">{{cite web |url= https://www.pbs.org/independentlens/documentaries/between-the-folds/ | work = Independent Lens | title = History of Origami |publisher=[[PBS]] |access-date=13 March 2012}}</ref>), which has become the standard for most paperfolders. The publishing of this book helped Yoshizawa out of his poverty. It was followed closely by his founding of the International Origami Centre in Tokyo in 1954, when he was 43.<ref name="times-obit" />

His first overseas exhibition was organized in October 1955 by [[Gershon Legman]], a leading player in the early years of the origami movement. The exhibition was held at the [[Stedelijk Museum]] in Amsterdam.<ref name="times-obit" /> Felix Tikotin, a Dutch dealer, acted as a liaison.{{citation needed|date=February 2021}}

Yoshizawa lent many of his own origami models to other exhibitions around the world. He would never sell his origami figures,<ref name=":0">{{Cite AV media |title=[[Between the Folds]] |date=2008 |last=Gould |first=Vanessa |type=DVD}}</ref> but rather gave them away as gifts to people, and let other groups and organizations borrow them for exhibiting.

His second wife, Kiyo Yoshizawa, served as his manager and taught origami to the other patients where he was hospitalized until his death.<ref name = "Fox">{{cite web|last = Fox |first = Margalit | title = Akira Yoshizawa, 94, Modern Origami Master| url = https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9F07E4DC113FF931A35757C0A9639C8B63 | work = The New York Times|accessdate=13 March 2012|date=2 April 2005}}</ref>

== Technique ==
[[File:Wet-folding bull.jpg|thumb|A wet-folded origami bull]]
Although Yoshizawa pioneered many different origami techniques, [[wet-folding]] is one of his most significant contributions.<ref name="times-obit" /> This technique involves slightly dampening the paper before making a fold. Wet-folding allows the paper to be manipulated more easily, resulting in finished origami models that have a rounder and more sculpted look.

Wet-folding is most often used with thicker paper; normal origami paper is very thin and thus prone to tearing when using the wet-folding technique.<ref name = "About" /> Yoshizawa believed the process was the most important part. He is credited as saying, "When you fold, the ritual and the act of creation is more important than the final result. When your hands are busy your heart is serene".<ref>{{cite web |last1=Purser |first1=Cullen |title=The secret is folding: Grand Junction artist uses origami to quiet the mind |url=https://www.rmpbs.org/news/rocky-mountain-pbs/the-secret-is-folding-grand-junction-artist-uses-origami-to-quiet-the-mind |website=Rocky Mountain PBS |access-date=2 April 2026}}</ref>

== Later years ==
In March 1998, Yoshizawa was invited to exhibit his origami in the [[Carrousel du Louvre]] in France.<ref>{{cite news|title = Eric Joisel, French origami artist who mastered animal and human forms in complex paper-folded sculptures|url = http://www.ericjoisel.com/about_assets/times.pdf|newspaper = Times Newspaper|date = October 2010|access-date = 2015-10-02|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130118124840/http://www.ericjoisel.com/about_assets/times.pdf|archive-date = 2013-01-18|url-status = dead}}</ref> Although he had previously disliked his contemporaries, he was not opposed to having his photo taken with them. Many of his patterns had been diagrammed by his professional rivals, which angered Yoshizawa when he was younger.{{Citation needed| date= March 2012}} However, as he had aged, he found that he now enjoyed the company of his peers.

Yoshizawa died on 14 March 2005 in a hospital in [[Itabashi]], Tokyo, of complications from pneumonia, on his 94th birthday.<ref name = "Fox" />

After his death, he was featured in ''[[Between the Folds]]'', a documentary about origami that called him the father of modern, sculptural approaches to origami.<ref name=":0" />
